setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You are helping {lead|the} organize a team project day next month.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are planning a team project day with three coworkers.
pressure: {coworker3} says it is too much work to plan around everyone.
detail: The project day will include a working lunch.

tiers.1: A remark that demeans a coworker needs a response in the moment.
tiers.2: A plan that shuts someone out has to be fixed before anything else.
tiers.3: Scheduling should let everyone take part.
tiers.4: Assumptions about a person should be checked by asking them.
tiers.5: Drawing out every voice improves the plan once access is settled.

fact: During the planning meeting, {coworker3} jokes about the way {coworker2} speaks.
issues.action: Say calmly that the joke is not okay, and check in with {coworker2}.
issues.brief: say the joke is not okay and check on {coworker2}
issues.reason: Letting a demeaning joke pass tells the target it is acceptable. A calm response supports the coworker and sets a respectful norm.
issues.lesson: Respond calmly when a coworker is mocked; silence signals approval.

shortcut.text: Laugh along so the meeting does not get awkward.
shortcut.brief: laugh along to keep things light
shortcut.why: Laughing along joins in the disrespect and leaves the coworker unsupported.
shortcut.mis: Avoiding awkwardness is more important than addressing disrespect.

fact: {coworker} uses a wheelchair, and the planned meeting room is up a flight of stairs.
clear: The project day was already moved to a ground-floor room.
issues.done: the project day was already moved to an accessible room
issues.action: Suggest moving the project day to a room everyone can reach.
issues.reason: A plan that a teammate cannot physically join shuts them out. Choosing an accessible room includes everyone.
issues.lesson: Plan events so every team member can take part fully.

shortcut.text: Plan for {coworker} to join by video from downstairs.
shortcut.why: Video from another floor leaves {coworker} outside the group when an accessible room would include them.
shortcut.mis: Offering a lesser alternative is the same as including someone.

fact: The planned date falls on a religious holiday that {coworker2} observes.
clear: {coworker2} checked the calendar and confirmed the date works.
issues.done: the date was already checked with {coworker2}
issues.action: Suggest checking possible dates with the whole team before choosing one.
issues.brief: check possible dates with the team
issues.reason: Picking a date some people cannot attend leaves them out. Checking dates is a simple way to respect everyone.
issues.lesson: Respect differences in how people observe holidays when scheduling team events.

shortcut.text: Keep the date and let {coworker2} decide whether to come.
shortcut.why: Keeping a date that conflicts with a coworker's observance puts them in an unfair position.
shortcut.mis: Team events should not change for one person.

fact: You realize you planned to give {coworker} only the note-taking without asking what they would prefer.
issues.action: Ask {coworker} which part of the project they would like to take on.
issues.reason: Assigning roles based on assumptions can limit people unfairly. Asking respects their skills and choices.
issues.lesson: Notice your assumptions about people and check them by asking.

shortcut.text: Keep the plan, since note-taking is probably easiest for {coworker}.
shortcut.why: Deciding what is easiest for someone without asking is the assumption to avoid.
shortcut.mis: You know what suits others without asking.

fact: {coworker} has mentioned preferring to be asked directly before sharing ideas in a group.
issues.action: Invite {coworker} by name to share ideas for the project.
issues.brief: invite {coworker} by name to share ideas
issues.reason: People share ideas in different ways. Respecting a stated preference brings in ideas the team would otherwise miss.
issues.lesson: Adapt how you draw out ideas to the people on your team.

shortcut.text: Wait for {coworker} to speak up like everyone else.
shortcut.why: {coworker} told the team what works for them. Ignoring it loses their ideas.
shortcut.mis: Everyone should contribute in the same way.

proceed.text: Move ahead with the plan the team agreed on and share it with {lead|the}.
proceed.why: The plan includes everyone and nothing else needs addressing, so it is ready to go to the lead.
proceed.lesson: Once a plan works for everyone, move it forward.

generic.text: Plan everything yourself to save the team the trouble of discussing it.
generic.why: Planning alone leaves out the perspectives that make a team plan work for everyone.

generic.text: Choose whatever the majority of the team wants and move on.
generic.why: Going with the majority without checking can leave some teammates unable to take part.

overcaution.text: Survey every person at {workplace|the} before finalizing anything.
overcaution.why: The plan already works for the team. Surveying everyone delays it without need.
overcaution.mis: Asking more people always makes a plan more inclusive.

title: Draft invitation: team project day
intro: You drafted this invitation to the team. Check it before sending.
doc.lesson: Inclusive messages make it easy for everyone to take part and avoid assumptions.

lines.text: We are planning a team project day to reorganize the work area.
It will be in the ground-floor training room, which has step-free access.

bad.text: It will be in the upstairs storage room; everyone can manage the stairs.
bad.why: Assuming everyone can use stairs excludes people with mobility needs.

lines.text: Please reply with any dates that do not work for you.
lines.fine: Invites schedule conflicts before choosing a date.

bad.text: The date is set, so do not bother replying about conflicts.
bad.why: Refusing to hear about conflicts can exclude people who cannot attend.

lines.text: Lunch is provided; let me know about any food needs.
lines.fine: Invites people to share dietary needs.

bad.text: Lunch is pizza for everyone; no other options.
bad.why: Not asking about food needs can leave some teammates unable to eat.

lines.text: Tell me which part of the project you would like to take on.

bad.text: I have already given the heavy lifting to the guys and the decorating to everyone else.
bad.why: Assigning work by gender is a stereotype. People should choose roles based on their skills and preferences.

bad.text: Please keep your ideas normal so we do not waste time.
bad.why: Calling some ideas not normal discourages people with different perspectives from speaking up.

review.notes: Defects name stereotyped behavior only so students can identify it; no group is characterized.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, and you are the first person {client.plural} see when they come in.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are helping {client.plural} at the front of the {area}.
pressure: {coworker3} says to keep things moving fast.

tiers.1: A barrier that could hurt someone or keep them out comes first.
tiers.2: Communication has to work before service can.
tiers.3: Choices should be offered, not assumed.
tiers.4: Small courtesies, like a name said right, follow the bigger needs.
tiers.5: A disrespectful comment from a coworker can be addressed once the {client} is served.

fact: A {client} who uses a cane is waiting outside because boxes are blocking the ramp.
issues.action: Clear the boxes off the ramp right away and offer the {client} help coming in.
issues.brief: clear the ramp and offer help
issues.reason: A blocked ramp keeps the {client} out and could cause a fall. Clearing it fixes both problems.
issues.lesson: Keep access routes clear so everyone can get in safely.

shortcut.text: Tell the {client} to come in through the side door with the steps.
shortcut.brief: send the {client} to the stepped door
shortcut.why: Steps are harder for someone with a cane. The ramp exists so everyone has a safe way in.
shortcut.mis: Any entrance is as good as another.

fact: A {client} speaks limited English and looks confused, and {workplace|the} has a phone interpretation line.
issues.action: Offer the phone interpretation line so the {client} can be served clearly.
issues.reason: The interpretation line lets the {client} understand and be understood. Using it shows respect and prevents mistakes.
issues.lesson: Use the tools available to communicate clearly with people who speak other languages.

shortcut.text: Repeat your explanation more loudly and slowly.
shortcut.why: Volume does not overcome a language barrier and can feel disrespectful.
shortcut.mis: Speaking louder helps people understand another language.

clear: The interpretation line is already connected, and the {client} is following along.
issues.done: the interpretation line is already connected

fact: You notice you were about to steer an older {client} away from the self-service screen without asking.
issues.action: Offer both the screen and in-person help, and let the {client} choose.
issues.brief: offer both options and let them choose
issues.reason: Assuming what someone can do because of their age is a bias. Offering choices treats them as an individual.
issues.lesson: Offer choices instead of deciding for people based on assumptions.

shortcut.text: Handle everything for the {client}, since that is probably easier for them.
shortcut.why: Deciding for someone based on age is the assumption to avoid.
shortcut.mis: Helping without asking is always kind.

fact: You are not sure how to pronounce the {client}'s name on the paperwork.
issues.short: the name you are unsure how to say
issues.action: Politely ask the {client} how to say their name.
issues.brief: ask how to say the name
issues.reason: Asking shows respect. Guessing or avoiding the name can feel dismissive.
issues.lesson: When unsure how to say someone's name, ask politely.

shortcut.text: Avoid using the {client}'s name at all so you do not get it wrong.
shortcut.why: Avoiding someone's name can feel cold. A polite question solves the problem.
shortcut.mis: Avoiding a name is more respectful than asking.

fact: Once the {client} leaves, {coworker3} imitates the {client}'s accent.
issues.action: Tell {coworker3} privately that mocking how someone speaks is not okay.
issues.brief: tell {coworker3} privately it is not okay
issues.reason: Mocking {client.plural} creates a disrespectful workplace even when they are not present. A private word addresses it directly.
issues.lesson: Speak up about disrespect toward the people you serve, even when they are not present.

shortcut.text: Ignore it, since the {client} did not hear the comment.
shortcut.why: Disrespect is not acceptable just because the target cannot hear it. It shapes how the team treats people.
shortcut.mis: A comment is harmless if the person never hears it.

proceed.text: Help the {client} the way you would help anyone, and complete the visit.
proceed.why: Nothing stands in the way of good service here, so helping the {client} as usual is right.
proceed.lesson: Respect shows in consistent, attentive service for every person.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to take over this {client} because the visit feels awkward.
generic.why: Handing off someone because of a difference in need or background treats them unequally.
generic.mis: Passing someone to a coworker avoids problems.

generic.text: Rush through the visit so the waiting {client.plural} do not get upset.
generic.why: Rushing one person because others are waiting gives them worse service.
generic.mis: Speed matters more than each person's experience.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, helping a {client} at the front of the {area}.

ramp: Boxes have been left on the ramp to the entrance.
language: The {client} you are helping speaks limited English.

steps.text: Move the boxes off the ramp
Greet the {client} and ask how you can help
Confirm the {client} has what they need

rel: The {client} needs to be able to get in first.
Greeting first shows you are there to help, then you bring in the interpreter.
The request has to be understood before you can help with it.
You find out the request before helping.
process.lesson: Remove barriers, communicate in a way that works, help, and confirm.

review.notes: Interpretation line stated as a workplace resource. Age assumption is framed as the student's own bias to check.
